body.objective: Students will be able to analyze harmony with Roman numerals.
body.iCan: I can analyze harmony with Roman numerals.
successCriteria: I can label chords in a major key with Roman numerals
I can analyze progressions in real songs
I can explain the function of tonic, subdominant and dominant chords
body.hook: Thousands of hit songs use just four chords. Musicians can hear a song once and play along because they recognize the progression. Roman-numeral analysis is the tool that makes this possible: it describes chords by their role in a key, not by their names.

vocabulary.definition: Labelling chords by their scale degree in a key.
The home chord of a key; it feels stable and resolved.
The chord on the 4th degree; it moves away from home.
The chord on the 5th degree; it creates tension that pulls back to I.
A chord progression that ends a phrase.
Belonging to the notes of the key.

study.title: Hearing the Hidden Structure
study.question: How does harmonic analysis reveal how songs work?
study.passage:
Chords in C major (built on each scale degree):
I C major · ii D minor · iii E minor · IV F major · V G major · vi A minor · vii° B diminished
Upper-case = major, lower-case = minor, ° = diminished.
Function:
• Tonic (I, vi): home, rest
• Subdominant (IV, ii): moving away
• Dominant (V, vii°): tension, wants to return to I
Cadences:
• Perfect (authentic): V–I, sounds final
• Plagal: IV–I, the "Amen" cadence
• Half: ends on V, sounds unfinished
• Deceptive: V–vi, a surprise
Common progressions: I–V–vi–IV (C–G–Am–F), I–IV–V–I, ii–V–I (jazz), I–vi–IV–V (1950s doo-wop).
Part 1 (15 minutes): Label progressions in C, G (G Am Bm C D Em F♯°) and F major.
Part 2 (15 minutes): Listen to four songs chosen by the teacher and identify which common progression each uses.
Part 3 (15 minutes): Transpose I–V–vi–IV into three keys and play it on keyboard or guitar.
